title: Agreement and construction according to sense
summary: Application explanation: Smyth distinguishes ordinary concord from construction according to sense and attraction. These categories require examination of the actual construction.
canEstablish: A mismatch in grammatical gender can be identified and compared with documented agreement according to sense.
cannotEstablish: A gender mismatch alone cannot rule out a referent or decide whether a command addresses nations corporately or people within them.

title: Personal pronouns according to sense: Matthew 28:19
summary: Application explanation: In his discussion of personal pronouns according to sense, Robertson explicitly relates αὐτούς in Matthew 28:19 to ἔθνη. He compares other pronoun usages involving grammatical and natural gender.
canEstablish: A documented grammarian treats the masculine pronoun as referring to the neuter noun; grammatical gender alone does not make that reference impossible.
cannotEstablish: This observation does not independently establish a corporate political, covenantal, or exclusively individual interpretation, or any baptismal policy.

title: Grammatical and natural gender
summary: Application explanation: Greek has masculine, feminine and neuter grammatical gender. Grammatical gender and the sex or personhood of a referent are distinct; masculine forms may designate mixed classes.
canEstablish: Gender is a feature of the annotated Greek form, useful for agreement checks.
cannotEstablish: Neuter does not mean inanimate and masculine does not mean only male persons. Gender cannot by itself determine the social extent of a referent.

title: Number
summary: Application explanation: Singular, dual and plural are inflectional categories. The NT annotations in this pack primarily distinguish singular and plural.
canEstablish: The form can be classified as singular or plural in the supplied analysis.
cannotEstablish: Plural alone cannot decide between collective and distributive interpretations, or count the people intended.

title: Case and agreement
summary: Application explanation: Case constrains syntactic relations; the subject of a finite verb is ordinarily nominative, and apposition involves case concord. Each construction still requires syntactic analysis.
canEstablish: Case can constrain candidate syntactic relations when combined with verb and clause structure.
cannotEstablish: An accusative is not always a direct object, and a genitive does not by itself select one English relationship or theological conclusion.

title: Person and number in finite verbs
summary: Application explanation: Finite verbs ordinarily agree with their subjects in person and number.
canEstablish: A second-person plural finite form addresses a plural grammatical subject.
cannotEstablish: Person and number do not identify all implied participants or the scope of every later application of a command.

title: Aorist and duration
summary: Application explanation: Smyth describes the aorist indicative as presenting a past event without specifying how long it occupied. Other moods must not be assigned past time merely from the aorist stem.
canEstablish: An aorist annotation identifies the tense stem; context and mood determine its use.
cannotEstablish: Aorist does not itself establish instantaneous, once-for-all or unrepeatable action. An aorist imperative is not thereby a past-time command.

title: Voice
summary: Application explanation: Voice describes the relation of the subject to the verbal action. Middle and passive forms and meanings need to be distinguished in context.
canEstablish: The upstream analysis supplies an active, middle or passive classification.
cannotEstablish: A voice label alone cannot decide the identity of an unexpressed agent or whether a traditional deponent label resolves the semantics.

title: Mood and verbal nouns
summary: Application explanation: Greek distinguishes indicative, subjunctive, optative and imperative; infinitives and participles are verbal nouns in the traditional classification.
canEstablish: The annotation identifies a formal category for interpreting the clause.
cannotEstablish: An imperative alone does not identify every intended recipient; a participle does not automatically mean a temporal sequence or a second independent command.

title: Parts of speech and verbal forms
summary: Application explanation: Inflected forms must be interpreted in their phrase and clause; participles combine verbal and nominal properties.
canEstablish: The imported part-of-speech category supports a plain-language parse.
cannotEstablish: A part-of-speech tag alone cannot supply a missing argument, word sense or discourse function.
